sentences.text: Metriorhynchus was a marine reptile belonging to the family Metriorhynchidae, a group characterized by tail anatomy that supported a shark-like tail fluke. These animals averaged about 3 meters in length, a size comparable to many modern crocodiles. However, their bodies were much more streamlined and tapered with a finned tail, making them significantly more efficient swimmers than their modern crocodile relatives.

Unlike many pseudosuchians, which typically possess extensive bony shields known as osteoderms, Metriorhynchus lacked these features and likely had smoother skin similar to plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs.

No eggs or nests of Metriorhynchus have been found, leaving its life cycle largely unknown compared to other Mesozoic marine reptiles like plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs that are known to give live birth at sea.

Recent examination of fossil specimens revealed that adults possessed well-developed glands to eliminate excess salt, meaning they could likely drink seawater and eat prey with the same ionic concentration as the surrounding ocean without dehydrating.
The genus Metriorhynchus was established by Christian von Meyer in 1832, with the type species designated as Metriorhynchus brevirostris.
The type species M. brevirostris was originally named in 1829 as a species of Steneosaurus before being elevated to a separate genus in 1832.
Hua & Tabouelle (2026) identified a skull from Kimmeridgian strata at Cap de la Hève in Normandy, France, as belonging to the species M. palpebrosus.

Metriorhynchus was a predator that spent most, if not all, of its life in the sea. As a versatile and opportunistic hunter, it targeted armored belemnites, fast and elusive fish, and larger species like the filter-feeder Leedsichthys.
It occasionally likely tried to capture flying animals like pterosaurs and fed on plesiosaur carcasses found on the sea floor.
Metriorhynchids had hip anatomy conducive for live birth, a trait evidenced in the related Dakosaurus.

Despite being an effective predator, it remained vulnerable to larger predators of its time, such as the pliosaur Liopleurodon, which could reach over 10 meters in length. Because it had lost the osteoderms characteristic of other crocodiles to become more efficient swimmers, it likely had few natural defenses against these larger marine predators.
Only one valid species is currently recognized, the type species M. brevirostris, which was formerly known as M. geoffroyii.
Young et al. (2019) synonymized M. geoffroyii with M. brevirostris and reassigned the specimen MNHN.F.RJN 116 to M. brevirostris.

Studies published since 2010 found that short-snouted metriorhynchines previously assigned to Metriorhynchus are distinct genera. Two long-snouted species, M. acutus and M. leedsi, have been reclassified into the genus Gracilineustes, while all short-snouted species have recently been transferred to the genera Purranisaurus and Suchodus.
The genus lived from the Bathonian to the Tithonian stages, between 168.2 and 143.1 million years ago.
There are 30 recorded fossil occurrences of the genus.
Recent phylogenetic analyses do not support the monophyly of Metriorhynchus, a view held from the 1860s to 2010. However, some long-snouted forms appear to form a natural group.
It is currently unknown whether Metriorhynchus performed mating on land or in the sea.
